title: Typed values in C#
summary: Use a typed list and a foreach loop to count positive values.

scenario.briefing: The campus store reconciles stock changes from several suppliers. Count the positive changes in C#.

objectives.description: Apply the taught syntax in a working file.

hints: The loop already visits each value.
Test whether the value is greater than zero.
Increment count inside the if body.

misconceptions.testDescription: The foreach loop counts only positive values.
misconceptions.feedback: count += 0 never changes the count. Increment in the positive branch.

misconceptions.description: Assuming nullable annotations enforce runtime checks.
misconceptions.feedback: Annotations describe intent to the compiler. Runtime JSON and database values still need validation.

sections.title: C# values and decisions
sections.body: C# declares values with a type: int count = 3; double price = 12.50; bool ready = true; and string name = "Ada";. Value types store their data directly; reference types refer to objects. Nullable reference types make absence explicit. if and switch select branches, and pattern matching can test shape and type. A foreach loop visits every element: foreach (int value in values) { ... }.

statements.label: List<int> stores elements with a compile-time element type.
A value-type variable contains its data directly.
A non-nullable string can still be null at runtime without a warning.
A foreach loop can visit a List<int> without an index.
